hero.title: Choose Your Product-Building Approach.
hero.intro: Use your MVP scope, essential features and user flow to choose a bounded build approach with explicit trade-offs and unknowns.

fields.label: MVP scope, essential features and user-flow references from Lessons 41–43
Learning question, time/skills/resource limits, data/access needs and unresolved conditions
At least two feasible approaches: manual/service, clickable prototype, no-code/low-code or custom/hybrid; suitability and limits
Approach | task/flow fit | effort status | skills/ownership | data/integrations | accessibility | maintenance/exit risks
Chosen approach and reasons tied to the task; rejected alternatives and trade-offs
What this approach will simulate, implement or exclude; safeguards and capability unknowns
Dependencies to review, responsible owner, acceptance checks and revisit/stop conditions
Lesson 45 prototype plan: task/screens or service steps, resources, time boundary and testable learning question
Did familiarity, hype or sunk effort influence your approach more than task fit?
What evidence or constraint could favour a simpler or different approach?
Which capability, data/access requirement or dependency must be reviewed before implementation?

questions.prompt: What should drive the build approach?
options: The scoped task, learning question and constraints
questions.explanation: Choose for task fit and reviewed constraints.

questions.prompt: What can a clickable prototype establish by itself?
options: A simulated navigation path, with usability still to be tested
questions.explanation: Keep simulated behaviour distinct from actual capability.

questions.prompt: A needed integration is unverified. What belongs in the strategy?
options: Mark it unknown, assign review and define a revisit condition
questions.explanation: Document dependencies before relying on them.

sections.label: 01 / WATCH
sections.heading: Which approach fits your task and constraints?

scenes.title: Start with the flow
scenes.visual: Scope, feature matrix and user-flow cards
scenes.narration: You have scoped the MVP, prioritized features and mapped the customer task. Now choose an approach that supports that task and learning question. Choosing a tool is not the same as proving demand.

scenes.title: Compare approach types
scenes.visual: Manual, clickable, no-code and custom cards
scenes.narration: A manual service lets a person perform work. A clickable prototype simulates navigation. No-code and low-code use configured components. Custom or hybrid development offers another route. Each has limits; none is automatically best.

scenes.title: Use your constraints
scenes.narration: Compare flow fit, resources, skills, data needs, integrations, accessibility and maintenance. Mark effort unknown where it has not been reviewed. Do not invent tool capabilities or prices.

scenes.title: Explain the choice
scenes.narration: For a fictional registration-route task, a clickable prototype may help explore navigation before building real registration. It cannot test payment, real accounts or production reliability. A manual service would answer a different operational question.

scenes.title: Check dependencies and exit
scenes.narration: Name what needs verification, who will review it and when you will reconsider. Check access, data, export, maintainability and vendor dependencies before real implementation. Do not hide safeguards to make an approach look easier.

scenes.title: Prepare the first prototype
scenes.narration: Export your Build Strategy with the chosen approach, trade-offs and prototype boundaries. Lesson 45 uses it to create your first prototype. Lesson 46 then tests prototype usability. This strategy is a plan, not an implemented product.

sections.label: 02 / LEARN
sections.heading: Choose for the next learning task.

children: A
build approach
describes how you will create the scoped experience. A
prototype
represents enough behaviour to explore a question.
No-code/low-code
uses configured components with different degrees of coding. A
hybrid
combines approaches. An
exit plan
explains how you could move data or work if the approach changes.
Objective:
compare at least two feasible approaches and choose one with explicit boundaries.
Why it matters:
committing to a tool too early can spend resources on capabilities your task does not need.
Generic approach comparison — verify fit for your context
Approach
Useful for
Limits to examine
Manual/service
Learning how a service or operation works through people
Capacity, consistency, handling data, repeatability
Clickable prototype
Exploring a screen/navigation task
Simulated behaviour; no actual accounts, payments or reliability proof
No-code/low-code
Configuring a workflow where reviewed components fit
Platform capability, permissions, export, integrations and ongoing costs
Custom/hybrid
Building behaviour requiring an owned implementation
Skills, maintenance, reviewed effort and security/data responsibilities
Review Lessons 41–43 and unresolved Validate conditions manually.
Name the task and learning question; list resources and constraints.
Compare at least two feasible approaches with evidence/source status.
Choose for task fit; mark effort and capabilities unknown until reviewed.
Record simulations, exclusions, safeguards, owners and revisit conditions.
Pass a bounded prototype plan into Lesson 45.
Fictional example

A clickable registration-route prototype may help explore navigation from invitation to destination. A manual concierge approach may help explore service handling instead. Choose the clickable option for a navigation question; keep payment, accounts and production integrations excluded. No usability findings or technical estimates exist yet.

options.label: Build every production integration first
options.feedback: Production integration work is not necessary to explore a simulated navigation question.

options.label: Plan a scoped prototype and later usability check
options.feedback: Plan enough interaction to explore route comprehension; test usability later without pretending integrations exist.

children: A plan is not implementation. Lesson 45 creates the prototype; Lesson 46 tests usability. Actual technology/integration planning and security principles follow in Lessons 48–49.
